notes: Pick in batches: carts by shortest walk, zone, rush, carrier & service, or customer

entries.title: Pick in batches: carts by shortest walk, zone, rush, carrier & service, or customer
items: The pick queue builds carts for you, five ways: Shortest walk (orders that save real walking together), Zone (one zone per cart, orders needing two zones kept whole), Rush & due (rush carts first, all rush), Carrier & service (UPS Ground and UPS 2nd Day Air on their own carts, each carrier with its services as rows) and Customer. Keep each customer apart works with all of them.

Each group is one row: “67 orders → 6 carts”, Cart 1 of 6 with its stops and how much less walking it is, and Start cart 1. See all carts lists the rest. Carts hold up to 12 orders, never mix packing types, and are built from the whole queue — fast at thousands of orders.
The filters (date, status, customer, zone, packing and the new Carrier filter) now sit on Orders to pick, the list they narrow. Ticking orders to build your own cart works as before.
The handheld pick screen has the same Pick in batches, folded into one line above the scanner.

entries.title: File drops: placards, slips and print files straight to Switch — by SFTP, S3 or a folder
items: Settings → File drops writes documents as the work happens to a folder, an SFTP server or an S3 bucket, for Enfocus Switch (or any hot folder) to route to the right printer and tray. Owners and admins set it up; Add and test tries each destination straight away.

Tick what drops, each with its own settings: placards when stock lands in a location (receiving, moves — or a license plate's placard, once, instead of one per SKU); pick slips when an order is ready to pick or picking starts, in pick-queue order (rush first), plus the batch's slip when a batch pick opens; pack slips when packing starts or the order is packed; print-ready PDFs for print-on-demand and direct mail jobs when they're ready or go to press; scheduled reports as they're emailed.

File names and folders are patterns — {seq}, {order}, {customer}, {carrier}, {location}, {sku}… — with an example under each drop. A job ticket (XML) can land beside each file with the customer, order, carrier, rush, ship-by and quantity, for Switch to route on.

Files arrive whole (written then renamed into place), within about five seconds. If a destination can't be reached, files wait and try again with the reason shown; Sent lists every file, with Send again. SFTP servers are pinned to the key seen on the first test.
A drop starts from the moment it's switched on — nothing that already happened is sent. In a test world, file drops stay off unless switched on there.

entries.title: BCC Architect Web Services, USPS address correction at checkout, and Intelligent Mail barcodes for comingled mail
items: Amphora now makes the Intelligent Mail barcode (IMb) for mail that isn't presorted — comingled, or mailed as it is. Enter your Mailer ID under Settings → Direct mail → Mail barcodes; every piece gets a barcode with the mailing's Service Type ID, your Mailer ID, a serial number never used before, and the routing code from the checked address. The encoder matches every example in the USPS barcode specification.

Choose Basic or Full-Service, and what the USPS does with a piece it can't deliver — Standard treatment, Forward, Return, or Electronic address correction. Together with the mail class they pick the Service Type ID from the USPS table; Marketing Mail prints the matching endorsement (ADDRESS / RETURN / CHANGE SERVICE REQUESTED) below the postage area. Set the defaults for new mailings, and let clients choose the undeliverable option on their own mailings if you like.
The IMb manifest (CSV) on a mailing lists every piece's STID, Mailer ID, serial, routing code and bars — what a comingler asks for. Presorted mailings get the same STID from BCC Architect's presort.

BCC Architect Web Services: CASS and NCOA run with your BCC Architect licence (product key, add-on keys and NCOA login) on BCC's servers — the PS Form 3553 and NCOALink Processing Summary come back for the client. Amphora's barcodes always carry the full 11-digit delivery point from CASS.

Built-in address correction: when your BCC Architect licence is set up, every US address typed at portal checkout, in bulk checkout, in the API or saved to the address book is checked against the USPS's own data — corrected street, city and ZIP+4, a warning when the apartment number is missing, refused when the USPS doesn't deliver there. At checkout the buyer sees the corrected address and confirms it before the order is placed; bulk checkout checks every recipient up front.

Settings, where you'd look for them: BCC Software (built-in, Architect Web Services or REACH — only the chosen one's fields) is on Settings → Integrations; Settings → Direct mail has what's warehouse-wide (Mail barcodes, our postage permit); each brand's Direct mail — portal on or off, user groups, formats and price per piece — is on the brand, Customers → the brand → Direct mail. Print → Direct mail is just the work.
Fixed: a direct mail campaign's print SKU showed in the client's shop as a product. It's ordered through the mailing only.

entries.title: Direct mail: BCC Architect, a campaign page for clients, finishes, prices, postage and billing
items: CASS, NCOA and presort through BCC Architect. Enter your BCC Architect sign-in under Settings → Integrations → BCC Software, then Run with BCC Architect on a mailing: every address is CASS-certified and checked for movers, duplicates are dropped, and the presort sets the print order, barcode, tray and postage on every piece. The CASS (PS Form 3553), NCOA, summary and postage reports are kept on the mailing and shown to the client. You can also run BCC by hand with the input and import files.

Clients get a campaign page: a tracker with dates, one card saying what happens next, the list's results (accepted, changed, not mailing), the cost, and tabs for the piece, the artwork, every record on the list with why it was changed or rejected, the proof and the reports. Their campaigns list shows the artwork, results and cost of each.
Artwork by zone: clients drop images into the front, inside and message areas instead of building a PDF. Each image is checked as it lands, and a change after your OK makes the proof again by itself.

Finishes and prices: every mailing is matte, gloss or satin. Set each client's price per piece by format and finish under Prices per piece; clients see it when they start a mailing, and approving the proof locks it in. The previews show the paper and its finish.

Postage and billing: Mark mailed takes the postage from the USPS statement (filled in from the presort). The print — and the postage, on our permit — goes on the client's bill with the mailing's name, pieces and price on the invoice line. On their own permit, they see the postage but aren't billed for it. Clients get a postage report by sort level and rate.

Proofs make themselves. The moment a client has artwork and a list, they see a draft proof: six pieces with names and addresses from their file as uploaded, marked DRAFT, nothing to approve. Once we've passed the artwork and the list is processed, the final proof replaces it and waits for their approval — nobody has to press Make the proof (you still can, with 5 to 10 pieces).
Fixed: a direct mail print job no longer books order, pick, unit or print fees — the drop bills itself, so nothing is charged twice.

entries.title: The cart shows what's in each kit, and Direct mail in the client portal
items: Direct mail in the client portal, by user group. On the brand (Customers → the brand → Direct mail), turn it on for a brand, choose which of their user groups may use it (or everyone), and which formats they can choose. Their people start a mailing, upload the artwork (checked automatically right away) and their list, and send it to us. We check the artwork by hand and either send feedback, which they fix and send again, or mark it OK. Then we run the processing job (CASS, NCOA, duplicates, presort, list or ZIP order) and send a proof of 5–10 real pieces. They approve, and we print. Address checking stays on our side.

Print → Direct mail is now Pending and Processed. A job appears the moment a client or we start a mailing, with where it came from and the next step. The client's Direct mail page shows the same jobs their way: In progress and Mailed.

A kit in the portal cart now lists what goes in it: every part that always comes in the kit, then the buyer's picks, each with how many go in one kit. It also shows the count per kit and the total across the kits ordered. It used to be one cut-off line of picks. Long kits show the first six with Show all, and on a phone the list runs the full width under the line.

entries.title: Every CPU core, a floor that stays quick, updates you can undo, and card and label calls that happen exactly once
items: Placing an order, adding lines and creating a shipment no longer slow down as order history grows. Keeping the order search up to date used to read the whole search index on every change. With 97,000 orders that made each order about 4× slower than it should be, and it got worse every month. It now goes straight to the order's entry. The update applies in about a second, and search results are unchanged.

The nightly backup now copies one consistent snapshot of the warehouse on a background thread. Before, every scan or order during the backup made it start over, so on a busy floor a large warehouse's backup could run all night without finishing.
Copying the live warehouse into a test world works the same way, so it also finishes while people keep working.

Amphora now uses every CPU core on your server. It runs separate processes for the warehouse floor (scanners, staff screens, your API), for client portals, and for background jobs (backups, syncs, emails, snapshots). A portal rush only uses the portal processes' share, and heavy jobs never hold up a page. It's still one container, one port and one database file; how many processes run is sized to your server automatically. Settings → Health adds them all up. To go back to a single process, set AMPHORA_WORKERS=1.

Safe with several processes: every order, invoice, RMA, receipt, carton and SSCC number comes from one shared counter, so two can never get the same number. Stock checks and stock moves happen together, so stock can't go negative. A shipment, a cancel, an approval or a fee can't be done twice by two people at the same moment, card charges, refunds and labels are claimed before calling the processor or carrier, and a retried scan is still booked once.
Fixed: Settings → Health showed an error while an install's very first backup was running.

Floor first: a rush on your client portals can no longer slow the warehouse floor. Up to 16 portal requests are worked on at once. At a busy peak, any more get an immediate “This store is busy for a moment” page that tries again by itself after two seconds, and integrations get a “busy, retry” answer. Scanners, staff screens and your own API are never held back. Settings → Health shows how often it happened. Change the limit with AMPHORA_PORTAL_CONCURRENCY.

Scanning or typing a SKU code finds it instantly however big the catalogue is (it read every SKU on each such scan: 57 ms at 625,000 SKUs and growing). The Orders board's rush and overdue counts read only open orders, not the whole history (3.5 seconds → instant at 977,000 orders).

Client portals stay quick with a large order history. Every portal page and checkout worked out each product's open demand by reading the whole order history, about 9 seconds a page with 390,000 orders, and for that time the rest of the warehouse waited too. With 60 portals busy, scanners lost their connection. New indexes make it instant, including for popular products with a long history. The portal home page also counts a buyer's open, awaiting-approval and recently shipped orders directly instead of loading their last 500 orders, so the counts are now exact even past 500. The same update speeds up every pick and the order counts on the Orders board. It applies in about 25 seconds on a large warehouse.

Picking from a carton or pallet works. When the only stock at a location was inside a carton, the pick route sent pickers there, but the pick looked only for loose units on the shelf and refused every time, so the order could never finish. The route now names the carton, the scanner takes the units out of it, and the pick records which carton they came from. If someone moved the carton after the route was drawn, the scanner says so.

A card is never charged twice, a refund never paid twice, and a label never bought twice — even when the processor or carrier doesn't answer, or the server stops mid-call. Every such call is written down first. With no answer, the order waits as “payment unknown” (or the shipment as “label may have been bought”) and Amphora asks the provider what happened, then records it. A checkout cut off completely never leaves a half-order: it's cancelled and any money taken goes straight back. Providers that can't be asked (UPS, FedEx, Shippo, ShipStation) appear in Settings → Health for someone to settle. Fixed: after a carrier timeout Amphora said “the shipment is untouched — try again”, which could buy a second label.

Go back to the previous version from Settings → General → Updates. Amphora saves a copy of the database, switches to the version you ran before and keeps everything done since. If a version — newer or older — doesn't start, Amphora goes straight back to the one it was running and says why. Installs set up before this version: run install.sh update once on the server to get the new updater; install.sh use <version> also switches from the server.

Going back to the previous version is safe: it runs on the updated database and keeps everything done since, and receipt numbers and SSCCs carry on without repeats whichever way you go (Going back in the install guide). A test world started from Settings → Worlds now always runs its own backups and background work, and Settings → Health warns if background work hasn't run at all since Amphora started.

Amphora now records when it stops answering requests, and why: the longest pauses, the pages and database queries that caused them, and memory use. A pause that's still going on is written to the server log every 10 seconds, so even a server that never recovers leaves a record.

entries.title: The phase tracker, brought up to date
items: The roadmap map (/phasetracker) now shows where Amphora really is: ten stations in service — through Client Portals, Print & Kitting, Invoicing and the Compliance Pack — with the train at Platform & AI and Ship It mostly built.
Stations that are partly in service say what's still open (Amazon and ask-in-English reports; the Postgres option and onboarding templates), and Resolve & Horizon are the next stop.
The map uses the new brand colors and the Amphora mark, in Light and Dark.

entries.title: Your logo leads, and quiet release notices
items: Your company's logo now leads the top of the menu; Amphora moves to the foot of the menu.
A logo uploaded on a solid box (usually white) has the box removed automatically, with no halo, and its empty margins trimmed.

On the Forest menu, the sign-in panel and in Dark mode your logo is shown in a light version (its dark ink in Linen, colors as drawn) — or, if you prefer, on a small light plate. Choose under Settings → Branding, with a preview of both.

Release notices: after an update, a small card in the corner says what's new — once. Owners and admins also see, once, when a newer version is available, with its notes and (when this install can update itself) Update now.

entries.title: Amphora's new look
items: The warehouse app now follows the Amphora brand guide: a Forest menu, the new Amphora logo, Linen pages, white cards, Clay for the main action and Sage for where you are. Text is Inter, page titles are larger, and buttons, fields and table rows are taller and easier to hit.
Status colors are consistent everywhere: green done, amber needs attention, red stopped, blue in progress.
Scanner screens (/scan) are built for arm's length: bigger text, the location and quantity at 36px, and buttons at least 56px tall.
Keyboard focus now shows as a thick outline on every control, in Light and Dark.

Dark mode, done properly: System, Light or Dark from the header (and in Scan mode). System follows your device; your choice is kept on that device. Dark has its own colors from the brand guide, and printing is always Light.
Your accent color takes over the main buttons — adjusted automatically for Light and for Dark so the text on it always reads.
Client portals are unchanged — each keeps the look its brand designed, whatever a visitor's device is set to.
Pick slips, packing slips, count sheets, invoices and the Knowledge Base PDF use the new palette; the Knowledge Base PDF carries the new logo and is set in Inter.

entries.title: Safer under real conditions: counts, put-backs, payments, offline scanners, portal groups
items: Cycle counts: approval now applies the difference the counter actually found — counted minus what the system showed at the moment of the count — so picks after the count are never undone. A location that moved while it was being counted can only be recounted, and pick routes avoid locations waiting to be counted when other stock exists.

Put back: picked units from a cancelled order, a changed line, a reopened stop or a short close stay in staging until someone puts them back and confirms it (Upkeep → Put back, or right on the pick station). No shelf shows stock that's still on a cart.

Card payments: approved isn't paid. An order with an uncharged hold, a failed charge, or a charge the processor didn't answer can be picked but not packed, labelled or shipped until the payment is settled — or a billing person lets it ship with a reason.

Offline scanning is now a setting and off by default (Settings → General → Scanning). When on, a saved scan is only ever sent as the person who made it, with its real scan time; a refused one holds everything that person scanned after it until they say what they did on the shelf; managers see unresolved ones on Settings → Health.

Portal user groups: deleting a group with people in it asks where they go — another group, or suspended until one is assigned (browse, no ordering or approving). Switching a group off no longer opens its members up to the brand's open default.
Pick queue: find any order by number, customer or reference, however long the queue is.

entries.title: Pick faces that refill themselves, and picking from where you choose
items: Automatic pick replenishment: every SKU picked from a pick face gets a min/max rule, sized every night from its own picks — min covers the wait for a refill plus a safety margin, max a few days of picks, never more than the location holds. Upkeep → Pick replenish → Automatic rules.
Rules you set or edit yourself are never changed, a rule you switch off stays off, and nothing a client set (like a SKU's low-stock level) is touched.

The refill queue looks ahead: a pick face that won't cover the orders due in the next two days goes to the top, before faces that are merely below min. Refills only come from reserve in the same building.

Smarter pick locations: a pick face before reserve, one stop instead of several, the nearly-empty location cleared first, within reach before a lift — and two orders on one cart are never sent for the same last units.

Pick from another location: scan a different location that holds the product at a stop and the station offers to pick from there, or choose from the list. In the office, Pick from on the order sets the location per line.

entries.title: Health page, nightly backups, webhooks, and scanners that keep working offline
items: Settings → Health: one page that says whether the install is all right — disk space, database size, the last backup and restore drill, background work, email and webhook queues — and which pages and API calls are slow, grouped by route. It lists what needs attention and what to do.

Backups (Settings → Backups): Amphora backs itself up every night while work carries on, keeps 14 days, mirrors uploaded files, and can copy each backup to your own S3-compatible bucket off the machine.

Restore drills: every week (or on demand) the latest backup is unpacked and proved — unchanged since it was made, sound, complete, audit trail intact. Any backup can also be opened as a test world, or downloaded.
Settings → Backups → Secret key shows where the key that unlocks saved passwords lives, and lets an owner copy it into a password manager.

Webhooks (Settings → Webhooks): Amphora calls your other systems the moment an order is placed, ships or is cancelled, stock moves, or an invoice is issued. Every call is signed, failed calls are retried for a day, and a delivery log shows each answer. Brands can add their own from their API key.
A webhook can carry the login the receiving system needs (a bearer token or an API-key header), sent on every call next to the signature and kept encrypted.

Scanners keep working when the Wi-Fi drops: picks, counts and stock moves are saved on the device and sent by themselves when the connection is back — never booked twice. A bar at the bottom shows what's waiting, and anything the server then refuses, with the reason. Integrations get the same protection by sending an Idempotency-Key header.
Being picked by: the pick queue and the order page show who is working an order right now, and opening an order someone else is on warns you before you walk it.

Stock API for integrations that poll: every answer has a cursor and an ETag — send the cursor back (?after=) to get only what changed, or the ETag (If-None-Match) to get a quick 'nothing changed'. Works on the warehouse API and every portal API; a portal's stock answer now works out only the page asked for.
Fixed: a portal API key with Read stock acting as a buyer got an empty stock list. It now gets the stock for every product its group can see.

Name an ASN yourself: the ASN number on Announce inbound starts with the next system number and can be typed over with anything — a different prefix or suffix, the supplier's PO, a name. Rename it under Edit details until receiving starts. Leave it alone and the system number is used.
Fixed: the demo world could fail to rebuild after an update since 1.44.9 (its history was written before receipts went onto license plates).

A license that has run out can be renewed right on the stop screen: paste the key there, no need to reach Settings. Test worlds now run on the install's license instead of a trial of their own, and a newer key set in AMPHORA_LICENSE_KEY always takes over from an expired one.

entries.title: Rate limits and blocking addresses
items: Rate limits on by default: every API key, signed-in person and portal buyer gets its own allowance, so a client's integration polling too hard slows only itself. Over the limit, callers are told to wait (429 with Retry-After). Settings → Security → Network and rate limits.
Block an address or a whole range, for a set time or until removed. An address with repeated failed sign-ins or wrong API keys is blocked automatically for an hour.
Allow-lists: keep the warehouse app reachable only from your own networks while client portals stay open. Any API key can be limited to its owner's addresses.
Amphora now takes a request's address from the connection itself, so a forged header can't dodge a block. Behind a proxy on another machine, set AMPHORA_TRUSTED_PROXIES (see the install guide).
A client integration that retries an order while the first try is still going gets that order back, never a second one.
Settings → Security shows who has been rate-limited, the busiest callers, and addresses with failed sign-ins.

Warehouse API keys can be limited to what they're for: full access, or None, View or Change per area (catalog, inventory, orders, customers, billing, reports, integrations). A key outside its permissions is told exactly what it lacks.
A client's API docs page shows only what their key may do once they paste it.
Changes can't be made from another website: a page elsewhere can't use your signed-in session to change anything in Amphora.

Confirm it's you: before changing security settings, keys, people, single sign-on, invoices or test worlds, Amphora asks for your password or authenticator code if you haven't signed in or confirmed in the last 10 minutes. The change then goes through on its own.
Where you're signed in: Settings → Security lists every device on your account and signs any of them out, or all but this one. Admins can sign anyone out everywhere from Settings → People.
The audit trail is sealed: every entry is chained to the one before it, so any change, removal or insertion shows up. Reports → Audit trail → Check the trail hasn't been altered.

Keys needing attention (Settings → Security): every API key that has expired, is about to, or hasn't been used in months. Warehouse keys can have an expiry date, and keys nobody uses can be revoked automatically.
A portal person's own data: Export data downloads everything held about them; Erase… removes what identifies them for a deletion request, keeping orders without their name.

Searching orders stays fast with years of history: the search box now uses an index (same results, about 25 times faster on a busy install), and the ledger report opens instantly however long the ledger is.
The monthly invoice run and the daily storage count no longer hold up scanners and pickers while they work: the server answers the floor between customers.

entries.title: Built for a big warehouse: fixes from load testing
items: Two people can no longer pick the same stop on one order. The second scan says it’s already picked and to refresh the route, so the order never ends up with more on the cart than it needs and always ships.

Inventory and Locations open on any size of warehouse. Inventory pages through SKUs with stock 100 at a time; Locations shows one zone whole or every location 100 at a time, with a search for a location code.

The pick queue opens in about a second with thousands of open orders (it took 16 seconds and more). The table shows the 200 most urgent; counts, filters and suggested carts still cover the whole queue.

Faster everywhere as history grows: stock is now kept as running balances alongside the ledger, so receiving, allocating, picking, the portal's stock numbers and every stock screen read a few rows instead of a year of history. The ledger is still the record, and the balances are checked against it.
Low-stock alerts are right while orders are mid-pick. Picked units waiting in packing used to be counted twice until they shipped, so an alert could fire late or not at all.

entries.title: Lots kept apart when receiving
items: Receiving only suggests bins holding the same lot; other lots of the SKU are shown but never offered.
Lot codes that came in with the expiry stuck on (“MYZ91W - 08/01/2028”) are split into the lot and its expiry date — including the ones already imported.
